helplines.name: Carers UK Helpline
helplines.note: Advice for family carers. Weekdays 9am to 6pm.

helplines.name: Age UK Advice Line
helplines.note: Care, money and benefits. 8am to 7pm, every day.

helplines.name: Samaritans
helplines.note: Someone to talk to, day or night.

helplines.name: Alzheimer's Society Dementia Support Line
helplines.note: Dementia advisers and someone to talk to.

helplines.name: Stroke Association Helpline
helplines.note: For stroke survivors and their families.

helplines.name: British Heart Foundation Heart Helpline
helplines.note: Cardiac nurses for patients and families.

helplines.name: Macmillan Support Line
helplines.note: Cancer nurses and advisers. 8am to 8pm, every day.

helplines.name: Marie Curie Support Line

helplines.name: Diabetes UK Helpline

rotaJobs: Dealing with the council and benefits
Cover when the main carer is away

dementia.name: Dementia
dementia.title: Just diagnosed: dementia
dementia.lede: Your first 30 days after a dementia diagnosis, one step at a time.

items.text: Get the diagnosis in writing and a named contact
items.note: From the GP or memory clinic.

items.text: Save the helpline numbers
items.note: Admiral Nurses 0800 888 6678 · Alzheimer's Society 0333 150 3456

items.text: Tell the DVLA and the car insurer
items.note: Telling the DVLA is a legal requirement. Not telling them risks a fine of up to £1,000.

items.text: Ask the council for a free OT home assessment
items.note: An occupational therapist checks the home before any fall or crisis. See the Home safety kit.

items.text: Make both Lasting Powers of Attorney
items.note: Property and financial affairs, and health and welfare. Do it while they can still decide. If it's too late, see the No Lasting Power of Attorney kit.

items.text: Check their will is up to date
Claim Attendance Allowance
items.note: Not means-tested. Use the Benefits calculator to see what else may apply.

items.text: Ask the council about a council tax discount
items.note: Up to 100% off for severe mental impairment. It needs a GP certificate, and they must also get a qualifying benefit such as Attendance Allowance, so claim that first.

items.text: Ask the council for a needs assessment and a carer's assessment
items.note: Both are free, whatever their savings.
links: Letter asking for a needs assessment

items.text: Ask about day centres and respite
items.note: Ask the social worker or council about day centres or day services: company, activities and a meal, often with transport, and a regular break for you. Many only take people referred by a social worker, so ask them directly; others let you book and pay privately. The council may help pay after a financial assessment. Ask about respite care too: short stays so you can rest or go away. Local dementia cafés and memory groups are often free: ask Alzheimer's Society or Age UK.

items.text: Check Carer's Allowance and Carer's Credit
items.note: Carer's Allowance needs 35 hours a week of caring, earnings under the weekly limit, and the person you care for must get a qualifying benefit such as Attendance Allowance. Check first: it can stop the severe disability extra in their Pension Credit, so ask Citizens Advice. Carer's Credit, from 20 hours a week, protects your State Pension.

items.text: Book a free fire safety visit
items.note: From your local fire and rescue service.

items.text: Tell your employer
items.note: One week of unpaid carer's leave a year, and the right to ask for flexible working, both from day one.

items.text: Ask the GP to record consent for you to discuss their care
items.note: A signed letter from your parent is enough in the early stages. If they agree, ask the surgery about proxy access in the NHS App too, so you can see letters and order repeat prescriptions.

parkinsons.name: Parkinson's
parkinsons.title: Just diagnosed: Parkinson's
parkinsons.lede: Your first 30 days after a Parkinson's diagnosis, one step at a time.

items.text: Ask for a Parkinson's nurse
items.note: Ask the neurologist or GP for a referral to a Parkinson's nurse specialist, your main contact between appointments.

items.text: Save the Parkinson's UK helpline
items.note: 0808 800 0303. Free advice from nurses and advisers.

items.text: Tell the DVLA and the car insurer
items.note: Parkinson's must be reported to the DVLA. Not telling them risks a fine of up to £1,000.

items.text: Ask the Parkinson's nurse about medicine timings
items.note: Ask what timings matter, and set phone reminders if that helps.

items.text: Ask for therapy referrals
items.note: Physiotherapy for movement and balance, occupational therapy for daily tasks, and speech and language therapy for speech or swallowing.

items.text: Ask the physio about exercise
items.note: Ask what's right for them, and about local Parkinson's groups.

items.text: Claim Attendance Allowance or PIP
items.note: Attendance Allowance if over State Pension age (usually once they've needed help for 6 months), Personal Independence Payment if under. Neither depends on savings. On the form, describe a typical bad day. Use the Benefits calculator.

items.text: Make both Lasting Powers of Attorney
items.note: Property and financial affairs, and health and welfare, while they can make the decision. If it's too late, see the No Lasting Power of Attorney kit.

groups.title: Weeks 3 to 4: home, care and you

items.text: Ask the council for a free OT home assessment
items.note: To reduce falls and make daily tasks easier. See the Home safety kit.

items.text: Plan for hospital stays
items.note: Parkinson's medicines need to be taken on time. If they go into hospital, tell staff their exact medicine times and take a written list. Parkinson's UK has free resources to help.

items.text: Ask the council for a needs assessment and a carer's assessment
items.note: Both are free, whatever their savings.
links: Letter asking for a needs assessment

items.text: Ask about day centres and respite

Ask about respite care too: short stays so you can rest or go away.

items.text: Check Carer's Allowance and Carer's Credit
items.note: Carer's Allowance needs 35 hours a week of caring, earnings under the weekly limit, and the person you care for must get a qualifying benefit such as Attendance Allowance. Check first: it can stop the severe disability extra in their Pension Credit, so ask Citizens Advice. Carer's Credit, from 20 hours a week, protects your State Pension.

items.text: Tell your employer
items.note: One week of unpaid carer's leave a year, and the right to ask for flexible working, both from day one.

items.text: Ask the GP to record consent for you to discuss their care
items.note: A signed letter from your parent is enough while they can decide. If they agree, ask the surgery about proxy access in the NHS App too, so you can see letters and order repeat prescriptions.

mobility.name: Poor mobility
mobility.title: Poor mobility and falls
mobility.lede: Your first 30 days of help when moving around gets harder, one step at a time.

items.text: Ask the GP for a falls check and a medicines review
items.note: Some medicines raise the risk of falls. Ask about the local falls prevention service.

items.text: Ask the council for a free OT home assessment
items.note: Equipment and small changes under £1,000 should be free in England.

items.text: Set up a fall alarm
items.note: See the Fall alarms and home cameras kit.

items.text: Make the home safer today
items.note: Remove loose rugs and clutter, add night lights, and keep a phone within reach.

items.text: Ask for a physiotherapy referral
items.note: Strength and balance exercises reduce falls. Ask about walking aids too.

items.text: Book an eye test and a hearing check
items.note: NHS eye tests are free for over-60s. Poor sight and hearing raise the risk of falls.

items.text: Claim Attendance Allowance or PIP
items.note: Neither depends on savings. On the form, describe a typical bad day. Use the Benefits calculator.

items.text: Apply for a Blue Badge
items.note: Parking close to where they need to go.
links: How to apply for a Blue Badge

groups.title: Weeks 3 to 4: bigger changes and you

items.text: Ask about a Disabled Facilities Grant
items.note: Up to £30,000 in England for a stairlift, level-access shower or ramp. Means-tested.

items.text: Check feet and footwear
items.note: Well-fitting shoes with a good grip help. Ask the GP about NHS podiatry.

items.text: Ask the council for a needs assessment and a carer's assessment
items.note: Both are free, whatever their savings.
links: Letter asking for a needs assessment

items.text: Ask about day centres and respite

Many only take people referred by a social worker, so ask them directly; others let you book and pay privately. The council may help pay after a financial assessment. Ask about respite care too: short stays so you can rest or go away.

items.text: Make both Lasting Powers of Attorney
items.note: Plan ahead while they can make the decision. If it's too late, see the No Lasting Power of Attorney kit.

items.text: Tell your employer
items.note: One week of unpaid carer's leave a year, and the right to ask for flexible working, both from day one.

items.text: Ask the GP to record consent for you to discuss their care
items.note: A signed letter from them is enough while they can decide. If they agree, ask the surgery about proxy access in the NHS App, so you can see letters and order repeat prescriptions.

stroke.name: Stroke
stroke.title: After a stroke
stroke.lede: Your first 30 days after a stroke, one step at a time.

groups.title: Week 1: in hospital and coming home

items.text: Ask the stroke team what to watch for
items.note: Ask what signs mean you should call 999, and write it down. The NHS website explains stroke symptoms.

items.text: Save the Stroke Association helpline
items.note: 0303 3033 100. Advice for stroke survivors and families.

items.text: Ask who is planning discharge, and for the plan in writing
items.note: See the Leaving hospital kit.

items.text: Ask about early supported discharge and rehab
items.note: Many areas offer therapy at home straight after hospital: physio, OT and speech and language therapy.

items.text: Stop driving and check the DVLA rules
items.note: They must not drive for a calendar month after a stroke, and must tell the DVLA if problems remain after that.

items.text: Keep a list of their medicines
items.note: Take it to every appointment. Ask the pharmacist or GP any questions about it.

items.text: Ask about a 6-month review
items.note: Everyone should have a review about 6 months after a stroke. Ask the GP or stroke team.

items.text: Claim Attendance Allowance or PIP
items.note: Attendance Allowance if over State Pension age (usually once they've needed help for 6 months), Personal Independence Payment if under. Neither depends on savings. On the form, describe a typical bad day. Use the Benefits calculator.

items.text: Ask the council for a free OT home assessment
items.note: Equipment and small changes under £1,000 should be free in England.

items.text: Apply for a Blue Badge if walking is hard
items.note: See the Blue Badge kit. They can use it as a passenger too.
links: How to apply for a Blue Badge

items.text: Ask the council for a needs assessment and a carer's assessment
items.note: Both are free, whatever their savings.
links: Letter asking for a needs assessment

items.text: Ask about day centres and respite

eol.name: End of life care
eol.title: End of life care
eol.lede: Making the last months as comfortable as possible, and knowing what to do.

items.text: Ask the GP about palliative care
items.note: Ask for a referral to the local palliative care team or hospice. Hospices also support people at home.

items.text: Save the Marie Curie Support Line
items.note: 0800 090 2309. Practical and emotional support, for them and for you.

items.text: Ask the hospice about day services
items.note: Many hospices run day services with company and therapies, which also give carers a break. Ask about respite and night sitting too.

items.text: Ask about NHS Continuing Healthcare fast track
items.note: If health is declining quickly, the NHS can fund care urgently. The GP or nurse completes the form.

items.text: Ask about benefits under the special rules
items.note: If they may have 12 months or less to live, benefits such as Attendance Allowance can be paid faster at the highest rate. A doctor or nurse completes form SR1.

items.text: Talk about what matters to them
items.note: Where they want to be cared for, who they want with them, and any religious or cultural wishes.

items.text: Ask about an advance care plan
items.note: Ask the GP about a ReSPECT form or advance care plan, and whether they want a DNACPR decision recorded.

items.text: Check their will and Lasting Powers of Attorney
items.note: A will, and both Lasting Powers of Attorney, if not already made. If it's too late, see the No Lasting Power of Attorney kit.

items.text: Ask the GP to record consent for you to discuss their care
items.note: A signed letter from them is enough while they can decide. If they agree, ask the surgery about proxy access in the NHS App, so you can see letters and order repeat prescriptions.

items.text: Ask about equipment and night support
items.note: Hospital bed, commode, and night sitters from the hospice or Marie Curie.

items.text: Know who to call, day and night
items.note: Keep the numbers for the GP, district nurse, out-of-hours service and hospice in one place.

items.text: Ask about anticipatory medicines
items.note: Medicines kept at home in case symptoms such as pain or breathlessness appear suddenly.

items.text: Know what happens after a death
items.note: If the death is expected at home, you don't need to call 999: call the GP, out-of-hours service or hospice nurse to confirm the death. A medical examiner then reviews the cause of death, and their office tells you when you can register. Register within 5 days of that in England, then use Tell Us Once to inform government services.

items.text: Look after yourself
items.note: Cruse Bereavement Support: 0808 808 1677. You can ask for your own carer's assessment too.

heart.name: Heart failure
heart.title: Living with heart failure
heart.lede: Your first 30 days after a heart failure diagnosis, one step at a time.

items.text: Ask for a heart failure nurse
items.note: Ask the GP or hospital team for a referral. They are your main contact between appointments.

items.text: Save the British Heart Foundation helpline
items.note: 0808 802 1234. Advice from cardiac nurses.

items.text: Ask the nurse what checks to do at home
items.note: Ask what to record, and what changes to tell them about.

items.text: Ask when to call for help
items.note: Ask the GP or nurse when to call them, NHS 111 or 999, and keep the numbers in one place.

items.text: Keep a list of their medicines
items.note: Take it to every appointment. Ask the pharmacist or GP any questions about it.

items.text: Ask about cardiac rehabilitation
items.note: Supervised exercise and advice that helps people with heart failure feel better.

items.text: Ask about diet and drinks
items.note: Ask the heart failure nurse whether there is anything they should change.

items.text: Book flu, COVID and pneumonia vaccines
items.note: Free on the NHS for older people. Ask the GP or pharmacy.

items.text: Claim Attendance Allowance or PIP

copd.name: COPD and breathing
copd.title: COPD and breathing problems
copd.lede: Your first 30 days of help with COPD or another long-term breathing condition.

items.text: Ask for a written self-management plan
items.note: It says what to do on bad days, and when to call for help.

items.text: Save the Asthma + Lung UK helpline
items.note: 0300 222 5800. Advice from respiratory nurses.

items.text: Ask what to do on bad days
items.note: Ask the GP or nurse what the plan is if their breathing gets worse.

items.text: Check inhaler technique
items.note: Ask the pharmacist or practice nurse to watch them use their inhaler. Many people use them wrongly.

items.text: Ask for pulmonary rehabilitation
items.note: An NHS exercise and education course that improves breathlessness. Ask the GP for a referral.

items.text: Get help to stop smoking
items.note: The most important step if they smoke. Ask the GP or pharmacy about free NHS support.

items.text: Book flu, COVID and pneumonia vaccines
items.note: Free on the NHS for older people. Ask the GP or pharmacy.

items.text: Ask about home oxygen if it's been suggested
items.note: The specialist team explains whether it's needed and how it's set up safely.

cancer.name: Cancer
cancer.title: Supporting someone with cancer
cancer.lede: Your first 30 days after a cancer diagnosis, one step at a time.

items.text: Get the name of their key worker
items.note: Usually a clinical nurse specialist. Your main contact for questions.

items.text: Save the Macmillan Support Line
items.note: 0808 808 00 00. Help with treatment, money, work and feelings.

items.text: Ask for the treatment plan in writing
items.note: What treatment, where, how often, and what side effects to watch for.

items.text: Know who to call if they become unwell during treatment
items.note: Many hospitals have a 24-hour chemotherapy or oncology hotline. Save the number.

items.text: Claim Attendance Allowance or PIP
items.note: Attendance Allowance if over State Pension age (usually once they've needed help for 6 months), Personal Independence Payment if under. Neither depends on savings. On the form, describe a typical bad day. Use the Benefits calculator.

items.text: Ask about help with travel to hospital
items.note: The Healthcare Travel Costs Scheme refunds fares for people on low incomes. Hospitals may have volunteer drivers.

items.text: Check free prescriptions
items.note: Prescriptions are free in England for over-60s. Under 60, people having cancer treatment can get a medical exemption certificate: ask the GP or cancer team.

items.text: Ask Macmillan about grants and benefits advice
items.note: Macmillan offers one-off grants and free benefits advice.

items.text: Apply for a Blue Badge if walking is hard
items.note: Hospital parking can also be free or reduced. Ask the hospital.
links: How to apply for a Blue Badge

items.text: Ask the council for a needs assessment and a carer's assessment
items.note: Both are free, whatever their savings.
links: Letter asking for a needs assessment

sight.name: Sight and hearing loss
sight.title: Sight and hearing loss
sight.lede: Help for failing sight or hearing.

items.text: Book an eye test
items.note: Free on the NHS for over-60s. Opticians can visit at home if they can't get out.

items.text: Ask the GP for a hearing check
items.note: NHS hearing aids are free after an assessment.

items.text: Save the RNIB helpline
items.note: 0303 123 9999. Help with sight loss.

items.text: Save the RNID contact line
items.note: 0808 808 0123. Help with hearing loss and tinnitus.

items.text: Ask about a Certificate of Vision Impairment
items.note: An eye specialist can certify sight loss. They can then register with the council for support.

items.text: Ask the council's sensory team for an assessment
items.note: They can provide aids such as talking clocks, amplified phones and flashing doorbells.

items.text: Make the home easier to see in
items.note: Brighter bulbs, contrasting colours on steps and edges, and less clutter.

items.text: Keep hearing aids working
items.note: Ask the audiology clinic for free batteries and repairs.

items.text: Claim Attendance Allowance or PIP
items.note: Attendance Allowance if over State Pension age (usually once they've needed help for 6 months), Personal Independence Payment if under. Neither depends on savings. On the form, describe a typical bad day. Use the Benefits calculator.

items.text: Ask about the TV Licence
items.note: People registered blind or severely sight impaired get 50% off.

items.text: Ask about Blind Person's Allowance
items.note: If they're registered blind (severely sight impaired), they get extra tax-free income each year: tell HMRC. Being registered blind also qualifies them for a Blue Badge.
links: How to apply for a Blue Badge

items.note: Both are free, whatever their savings.
links: Letter asking for a needs assessment

continence.name: Incontinence
continence.title: Bladder and bowel problems
continence.lede: Practical help with incontinence. It's common, and often treatable.

items.text: Book a GP appointment
items.note: Incontinence often has a treatable cause, such as an infection, constipation or medicines.

items.text: Ask for a referral to the NHS continence service
items.note: Specialist nurses assess the problem and suggest treatment.

items.text: Ask which changes need a quick call
items.note: Ask the GP what changes you should tell them about the same day.

items.text: Ask about free continence products
items.note: After an assessment, the NHS may supply pads in some areas.

items.text: Ask about routines that might help
items.note: The continence nurse can suggest what's right for them.

items.text: Make the toilet easy to reach
items.note: A night light, clear path, raised toilet seat or commode. An OT can help.

items.text: Get a Radar key
items.note: Opens accessible public toilets across the UK. Disability charities and some councils sell them.

items.text: Don't pay VAT on continence products
items.note: Disabled people and people with a long-term illness can buy continence products without VAT. Ask for VAT relief when ordering.

items.text: Ask how to care for their skin
items.note: Ask the nurse or pharmacist what to use, and about any soreness.

items.text: Talk about it kindly
items.note: Use their words, keep it private, and focus on comfort, not blame.

items.text: Claim Attendance Allowance or PIP

diabetes.name: Diabetes
diabetes.title: Diabetes in older age
diabetes.lede: Help with diabetes as needs change in later life.

items.text: Ask for the diabetes care plan
items.note: What medicines, what targets, and what to do if they feel unwell.

items.text: Save the Diabetes UK helpline
items.note: 0345 123 2399. Advice from trained counsellors.

items.text: Ask about hypos
items.note: Ask the diabetes nurse what a hypo looks like for them and what you should do.

items.text: Ask about sick day rules
items.note: Some diabetes medicines need changing when someone is ill. Ask the GP or nurse.

items.text: Check the DVLA rules
items.note: If they use insulin, or have had a severe hypo, they may need to tell the DVLA. Search GOV.UK for “diabetes and driving”.

items.text: Book the yearly diabetes review
items.note: Blood tests, blood pressure, kidney check and a medicines review.

items.text: Ask about foot checks
items.note: Ask the nurse what to look out for, and make sure they have their yearly foot check.

items.text: Go to diabetic eye screening
items.note: Free every year or two. It finds damage before sight is affected.

items.text: Book flu, COVID and pneumonia vaccines
items.note: Free on the NHS for older people. Ask the GP or pharmacy.

items.text: Ask if their care plan still fits
items.note: Needs change with age. Ask at the yearly review whether anything should change.

items.text: Claim Attendance Allowance or PIP
items.note: Attendance Allowance if over State Pension age (usually once they've needed help for 6 months), Personal Independence Payment if under. Neither depends on savings. On the form, describe a typical bad day. Use the Benefits calculator.

items.text: Ask the council for a needs assessment and a carer's assessment
items.note: Both are free, whatever their savings.
links: Letter asking for a needs assessment

items.text: Check Carer's Allowance and Carer's Credit
items.note: Carer's Allowance needs 35 hours a week of caring, earnings under the weekly limit, and the person you care for must get a qualifying benefit such as Attendance Allowance. Check first: it can stop the severe disability extra in their Pension Credit, so ask Citizens Advice. Carer's Credit, from 20 hours a week, protects your State Pension.

items.text: Ask the GP to record consent for you to discuss their care
items.note: A signed letter from them is enough while they can decide. If they agree, ask the surgery about proxy access in the NHS App, so you can see letters and order repeat prescriptions.

arthritis.name: Arthritis
arthritis.title: Living with arthritis
arthritis.lede: Practical help when joint pain and stiffness make everyday life harder.

groups.title: Week 1: understand it and get support

items.text: Ask the GP which type of arthritis it is
items.note: Osteoarthritis and inflammatory types, such as rheumatoid arthritis, are managed differently. Ask whether a referral to a specialist is needed.

items.text: Save the Versus Arthritis helpline
items.note: 0800 5200 520, free. Information and support for people with arthritis and their families.

items.text: Ask the pharmacist for a pain relief review
items.note: Ask how and when to take their pain relief, and about anything that's making it hard to manage. The GP can review it too.

items.text: Ask who to contact if things get worse
items.note: Ask the GP or specialist team what changes to tell them about, and who to call between appointments.

groups.title: Weeks 2 to 3: movement and daily life

items.text: Ask for physiotherapy
items.note: Ask the GP for a referral. In some areas you can refer yourself to NHS physiotherapy. Ask about local exercise programmes for joint pain.

items.text: Ask the council for a free OT home assessment
items.note: An occupational therapist can suggest equipment such as grab rails, a perching stool, a raised toilet seat or kitchen aids. Equipment and small changes under £1,000 should be free in England.

items.text: Check feet and footwear
items.note: Supportive shoes help. Ask the GP about NHS podiatry if feet are painful.

items.text: Apply for a Blue Badge if walking is hard
items.note: See the Blue Badge kit.
links: How to apply for a Blue Badge

groups.title: Weeks 3 to 4: money, bigger changes and you

items.text: Claim Attendance Allowance or PIP
items.note: Attendance Allowance if over State Pension age (usually once they've needed help for 6 months), Personal Independence Payment if under. Neither depends on savings. On the form, describe a typical bad day. Use the Benefits calculator.

items.text: Ask about a Disabled Facilities Grant
items.note: Up to £30,000 in England for a stairlift, level-access shower or ramp. Means-tested. See the Home safety kit.

items.text: If a joint replacement is suggested
items.note: Ask about waiting times and what they can do to prepare. In England they can usually choose which hospital they're referred to for their first appointment.

items.text: Ask the council for a needs assessment and a carer's assessment
items.note: Both are free, whatever their savings.
links: Letter asking for a needs assessment

items.text: Ask about day centres and respite
items.note: Ask the social worker or council about day centres or day services: company, activities and a meal, often with transport, and a regular break for you. Many only take people referred by a social worker, so ask them directly; others let you book and pay privately. The council may help pay after a financial assessment. Ask about respite care too: short stays so you can rest or go away.

items.text: Check Carer's Allowance and Carer's Credit
items.note: Carer's Allowance needs 35 hours a week of caring, earnings under the weekly limit, and the person you care for must get a qualifying benefit such as Attendance Allowance. Check first: it can stop the severe disability extra in their Pension Credit, so ask Citizens Advice. Carer's Credit, from 20 hours a week, protects your State Pension.

items.text: Ask the GP to record consent for you to discuss their care
items.note: A signed letter from them is enough while they can decide. If they agree, ask the surgery about proxy access in the NHS App, so you can see letters and order repeat prescriptions.

items.text: Tell your employer
items.note: One week of unpaid carer's leave a year, and the right to ask for flexible working, both from day one.

afterfall.name: After a fall or hospital stay
afterfall.title: After a fall or hospital stay
afterfall.lede: Getting back on their feet safely, and stopping it happening again.

items.text: Ask about reablement
items.note: Free short-term support at home, usually for up to 6 weeks, to rebuild confidence and skills.

items.text: Ask the GP for a falls check and a medicines review
items.note: Some medicines raise the risk of falls.

items.text: Set up a fall alarm
items.note: See the Fall alarms and home cameras kit.

items.text: Ask the physio what to do after a fall
items.note: Ask them to show you both, so you know the plan.

items.text: Ask for physiotherapy or a strength and balance class
items.note: Strength and balance exercises reduce falls.

items.text: Ask the council for a free OT home assessment
items.note: Equipment and small changes under £1,000 should be free in England.

items.text: Book an eye test
items.note: Free on the NHS for over-60s.

items.text: Check feet and footwear
items.note: Well-fitting shoes with a good grip.

items.text: Ask the council for a needs assessment and a carer's assessment
items.note: Both are free, whatever their savings.
links: Letter asking for a needs assessment

items.text: Ask about day centres and respite
items.note: Ask the social worker or council about day centres or day services: company, activities and a meal, often with transport, and a regular break for you. Many only take people referred by a social worker, so ask them directly; others let you book and pay privately. The council may help pay after a financial assessment. Ask about respite care too: short stays so you can rest or go away.

items.note: Attendance Allowance if over State Pension age (usually once they've needed help for 6 months), Personal Independence Payment if under. Neither depends on savings. On the form, describe a typical bad day. Use the Benefits calculator.

Check first: it can stop the severe disability extra in their Pension Credit, so ask Citizens Advice. Carer's Credit, from 20 hours a week, protects your State Pension.

items.text: Tell your employer
items.note: One week of unpaid carer's leave a year, and the right to ask for flexible working, both from day one.

items.note: A signed letter from them is enough while they can decide. If they agree, ask the surgery about proxy access in the NHS App, so you can see letters and order repeat prescriptions.

delirium.name: Sudden confusion (delirium)
delirium.title: Sudden confusion (delirium)
delirium.lede: Confusion that starts over hours or days needs urgent medical help. It is often treatable.

items.text: Get medical help the same day
items.note: Call the GP urgently or NHS 111. If you think it's an emergency, call 999.

items.text: Tell the doctor what's normal for them
items.note: Say how they were a few days ago, so the doctor can see what has changed.

items.text: Tell them about any recent changes
items.note: New medicines, a recent fall, or anything else that's different.

items.text: Ask the staff how you can help
items.note: Ask the GP, nurse or ward what you can do while they recover.

items.text: Bring their glasses and hearing aids
items.note: And familiar things from home, if they're in hospital.

items.text: Stay with them if you can
items.note: A familiar face is calming. In hospital, ask about open visiting for carers.

items.text: Share a This is me form in hospital
items.note: From Alzheimer's Society: tells staff about their routine, likes and how to calm them.

items.text: Ask what to expect
items.note: Ask the doctor how recovery is likely to go.

items.text: Ask the GP for a follow-up
items.note: Ask whether any further checks are needed once they've recovered.

items.text: Ask what to do if it happens again
items.note: Ask the GP, and write the plan down.

articles.title: Caring for someone with diabetes over Christmas: how to cope
articles.intro: The festive season can be busy and unsettled, which can make caring harder. This article is about you, the carer: staying organised, sharing the load and looking after yourself. For anything about their health, food or medicines, speak to their GP, diabetes nurse or pharmacist.

p: Christmas changes routines: visitors, travel, different mealtimes and services that close for the holidays. Writing down what's happening each day helps everyone know who's doing what.
list: Put family visits, and who's helping when, in a shared calendar.
Check when the GP surgery and pharmacy are closed over the holidays.
Order repeat prescriptions in good time.
Keep the diabetes team's contact details somewhere easy to find.

p: Caring through the holidays shouldn't fall on one person. Agree who covers which days, including lifts to appointments and collecting prescriptions. Kinav's calendar and reminders can help everyone keep track.

If you're unsure how changes in routine, food or activity over Christmas might affect them, ask their GP, diabetes nurse or pharmacist before the holidays. Writing your questions down first helps, and Kinav's Questions to ask can get you started.

list: For urgent advice, call NHS 111 or use 111.nhs.uk.
In an emergency, call 999.
Diabetes UK offers information and support for families.

p: It's normal to feel stretched at this time of year. Short breaks matter: ask family or friends to take over for an afternoon, and ask the council for a carer's assessment if you haven't had one.

articles.title: Caring for someone with COPD this winter: how to cope
articles.intro: Winter can be the hardest time for families living with COPD. This article is about you, the carer: how to stay organised, share the load and look after yourself. For anything about their health, speak to their GP, respiratory nurse, pharmacist or NHS 111. World COPD Day is on 18 November.

p: Living with someone's breathlessness can leave you on alert all the time, listening out at night and worrying when you're apart. That is very common, and it isn't a sign you're coping badly.
Naming the worry helps. Many carers find it easier once they know who to call and what the plan is.

list: Ask their GP or respiratory nurse whether they have a written plan for bad days, and ask for a copy for you.
Ask the professionals to explain, in their words, when to call them, when to call NHS 111 and when to call 999. Write it down.
Keep the GP, respiratory team, NHS 111 and pharmacy numbers by the phone and in your own phone.
Make sure family members have the same list.

sections.h: Questions to take to the next appointment
list: What should we expect this winter?
What changes should we tell you about, and how quickly?
Is there anything I can learn to help, and who could teach me?
Are they eligible for pulmonary rehabilitation, and can I come too?
Who do we contact out of hours?
Set up a shared family calendar for appointments, so you're not the only one keeping track. See the Appointments screen.
Agree a simple rota with family or friends for visits, shopping and lifts.
Ask the council for a needs assessment for them, and a carer's assessment for you. Both are free.
Ask about respite, so you can have regular breaks.

p: Keep up your own appointments, sleep and time away. Ask your GP whether you can get a free flu vaccine as a carer.
Talk to someone. The Asthma + Lung UK helpline is 0300 222 5800 for questions about living with lung conditions. Samaritans are on 116 123, any time, if it all feels too much.

sources.name: Asthma + Lung UK: contact the helpline

articles.title: Day centres: how they help your parent, and you
articles.intro: A day centre can be one of the simplest ways to make caring more manageable. Your parent gets company, activities and a hot meal, and you get a regular, reliable break. Here's what they offer, how to find one, and how to help the first visits go well.

sections.h: What happens at a day centre
p: Day centres are usually run by councils or local charities such as Age UK. Most are open on set days, often from mid-morning to mid-afternoon.
list: Company and conversation, with people of a similar age.
Activities such as music and singing, quizzes, gentle exercise, games, and arts and crafts.
A hot lunch and drinks through the day.
Transport to and from home, often by an accessible minibus. There may be a charge.
At some centres, extras such as hairdressing, foot care or help with bathing.
Some centres specialise in dementia care.

p: Many older people become lonely and less active when getting out is hard. A regular day out gives the week some shape and something to look forward to.

Being with others, joining in activities and having a proper meal can help them stay connected and more independent at home. Staff get to know them and can let you know if they notice anything has changed.
Caring with no breaks is exhausting, and it's one of the main reasons carers become unwell or give up work. A day centre gives you hours you can count on each week.
list: Go to work, or work without interruptions.
Go to your own appointments, or catch up on sleep.
See friends, or simply have time to yourself.
Know they're safe, fed and in company while you're apart.
Keep caring for longer, because you're not running on empty.

p: Many day centres, especially those run or funded by the council, only take people referred by a social worker. So the best first step is to ask the council's adult social care team for a needs assessment, and ask about day centres at it.

Other centres let you contact them directly and pay privately, and some offer a free taster day. Local charities such as Age UK, Alzheimer's Society and carers' centres often know what's available nearby.

Costs vary from place to place, and some charity-run sessions are free or low cost. If the council arranges it after a needs assessment, it may help pay, depending on a financial assessment of your parent's money, not yours.
If they pay themselves, benefits such as Attendance Allowance can be used towards the cost. Use Kinav's Benefits calculator to check what they may be missing.

sections.h: Questions to ask a day centre
list: Which days and hours are you open, and how much does it cost?
Is transport included, and what time are pick-up and drop-off?
What activities are there, and can they try a taster day?
What help can staff give, for example with the toilet, eating or medicines?
Are staff trained in dementia care, if that's needed?
How do you meet dietary needs?
What happens if they become unwell during the day, and how will you contact us?

sections.h: Making the first visits go well
p: It's normal for a parent to be unsure at first, and some say no straight away. A gentle approach helps.
list: Visit together first, or try a taster day.
Call it by what they'll enjoy, such as a lunch club or a music group, rather than “care”.
Start with a shorter day or one day a week, then build up.
Tell staff about their routine, likes and dislikes. For someone with dementia, a This is me form from Alzheimer's Society helps.
Label glasses, hearing aids, coats and bags.
Give it a few weeks. Many people come to look forward to their day.

p: If you need more than a day, ask the council about respite care: a short stay in a care home, or a carer staying at home, so you can rest or go away. Ask for a carer's assessment for yourself too. It's free, and it looks at what would help you keep going.

sources.name: NHS: carer breaks and respite care

kits.name: Preparing for a care needs assessment
kits.what: The council's free assessment: how to ask, how to prepare and what happens next. England.

steps.d: Contact adult social care at their council. Anyone who seems to need care has the right to an assessment, free, whatever their savings. Kinav can write the letter for you.
It can be at home, by phone or by video. They can have a family member or friend with them. If they'd struggle to take part and have no one to help, the council must offer an independent advocate.

steps.t: Keep a diary for a week
steps.d: Note what they need help with, day and night: washing, dressing, the toilet, meals, medicines, moving around, going out and staying safe. Include the bad days, not just the good ones.

steps.t: Write down what family do now
steps.d: List the help you and others give, and say clearly what you can't keep doing. The plan shouldn't assume family will cover everything.
A list of their medicines, GP and hospital contacts, recent letters from health professionals, and any equipment they use.
Many older people play things down. Let them speak first, then gently add what you've seen, using examples from the diary.
Ask whether they meet the national eligibility criteria, when you'll hear in writing, and for a copy of the assessment.
The council writes a care and support plan with you, and a financial assessment works out what they pay. With savings over £23,250 they usually pay the full cost at first.
The council must tell you why in writing and give information about other help, such as day centres or local charities. If you disagree, ask for a review or make a complaint.

steps.t: Ask for a carer's assessment too
steps.d: If you help them, you have the right to your own assessment, free. Kinav can write that letter too.
Age UK 0800 678 1602. Carers UK 0808 808 7777. Citizens Advice Adviceline (England) 0800 144 8848.

kits.name: Choosing a nursing home
kits.what: Shortlist, visit and ask the right questions.

steps.t: Ask the council for a free needs assessment
steps.d: It confirms what level of care is needed. Anyone can ask, whatever their savings.

steps.t: Work out how it will be paid for
steps.d: Use the Care costs tool. If savings are above £23,250 they will usually pay their own fees at first. Ask the council for a financial assessment either way.

steps.t: If their home is the main asset
steps.d: The value of their home is ignored for the first 12 weeks in a care home, and always if a partner or certain relatives still live there. Ask the council about a deferred payment agreement, which lets fees be paid from the home's value later, so it doesn't have to be sold straight away. The Society of Later Life Advisers can find an accredited adviser.

steps.t: Check who can manage their money
steps.d: To deal with their bank, pension or the house, you'll need a property and financial affairs Lasting Power of Attorney. It can only be made while they can still decide. If it's too late, you can apply to the Court of Protection to become their deputy, which takes months. For benefits only, the DWP can make you their appointee. See the No Lasting Power of Attorney kit.
Use Find care, filter to nursing homes and dementia care if needed, and read each home's latest CQC report.

Say: "I'm looking for a nursing place for my mum. Do you have a vacancy, what is the weekly fee, and what does it include?" Ask whether they keep residents if their savings run out and the council starts paying.
Go once at a mealtime. Look for staff talking with residents, call bells answered quickly, residents doing things, and a clean, fresh home.
How many nurses are on each shift? How much do you use agency staff? How do you support someone who becomes distressed? How often does a GP visit? Can residents stay here to the end of their life?

steps.t: Ask about NHS help with nursing costs
steps.d: In a nursing home, the NHS pays a weekly contribution towards nursing care, called NHS-funded Nursing Care, straight to the home. Check the fee quoted shows it. Ask about an NHS Continuing Healthcare check too: if they qualify, the NHS pays the full cost.
Use the Before you sign kit.

Bring familiar things and photos, label clothes, and tell the GP, pharmacy, bank, pension providers and the DWP about the new address. Ask whether they will stay with their GP or move to the home's GP. Check whether Attendance Allowance or PIP stops after 28 days if the council helps pay the fees.

kits.name: Setting up care at home
kits.what: Compare agencies and agree a care plan.

steps.t: Ask the council for a free needs assessment
steps.d: Ask about reablement too: free short-term support at home, usually for up to 6 weeks.
If the council helps pay, you can ask for the money as a direct payment and choose the agency or carer yourself, instead of the council arranging it.
Write down the times of day and tasks, for example getting up and washed, lunch and medication, help to bed.

steps.t: Ask about day centres and respite
steps.d: Ask the social worker or council about day centres or day services, often with transport and a meal, and short respite stays so you can have a break. Many day centres only take people referred by a social worker. The council may help pay after a financial assessment.
Use Find care with "Care at home", and read each agency's latest CQC report.

Ask: What is your hourly rate, and is it higher at weekends? What is the shortest visit? Will Mum see the same carers? Are your carers trained in dementia care? What happens if a carer is late or can't come? How much notice do I give to stop?
Ask for the rates, terms and notice period by email before you agree.
The agency should visit first and write down what carers will do at each visit.

steps.t: Be there for the first visits
steps.d: Leave a notebook at home for carers and family to write in. A police-approved key safe lets carers get in if they can't answer the door.
Ask the council for a review if needs change.

kits.name: Arranging live-in care
kits.what: Find, check and plan cover for a live-in carer.

steps.d: A managed service employs the carer and must be registered with CQC. An introductory agency only introduces carers, so you take on more responsibility.
A live-in carer needs their own bedroom.
Ask for the weekly fee and put it into the Care costs tool to see how long savings last.

steps.t: Meet the carer before they start
steps.d: Ask the agency how they match carers, and what happens if it isn't working.
Ask who covers the carer's daily breaks, days off and holidays.
Let them know someone else will be living in the home.
Check the care plan still fits.

kits.name: Home safety and grants
kits.what: Free OT assessment, free equipment and grants.

steps.t: Ask for a free OT home assessment
steps.d: Call the council's adult social care team and ask for an occupational therapist to assess the home. Ask how long the wait is, and tell them about any falls or near misses, as this can speed things up.
In England, councils should provide equipment and small adaptations costing under £1,000 free of charge.

steps.t: Ask about a Disabled Facilities Grant
steps.d: Up to £30,000 in England for bigger changes such as a stairlift or level-access shower. It is means-tested, and usually needs an OT to recommend the work first. Don't start the work before it's approved, or it may not be paid. Tenants can apply too, with the landlord's permission.

steps.t: Book a free fire safety visit
steps.d: Your local fire and rescue service checks smoke alarms and fire risks.
Ask the council about telecare, such as a pendant alarm or fall detector. See the Fall alarms and home cameras kit.
Ask the council about its trusted trader scheme, and get 2 or 3 written quotes.

kits.name: Fall alarms and home cameras
kits.what: Get help quickly after a fall, and use cameras with care.

steps.t: Ask the council about a personal alarm
steps.d: Most councils run a telecare or lifeline service: a button worn on the wrist or neck that calls a 24-hour team. Ask during the needs assessment or OT visit. There is usually a weekly charge.

steps.t: Choose the right type of alarm
steps.d: A button they press; an automatic fall detector that calls for help even if they can't press it; a GPS alarm if they go out alone; or a smartwatch with fall detection. If they might forget to press a button, choose automatic fall detection.
Give the alarm service 2 or 3 people who live nearby and can get there quickly. Some services offer their own responders if family is far away.
A key safe by the front door lets responders and ambulance crews get in without breaking the door. Choose a police-approved model.
Most fall alarms are waterproof, so they can be worn in the shower, where many falls happen. Test it once a month.
Bed, chair and door sensors, or activity sensors that learn their routine, can alert you to a fall or a night-time wander without filming them.

steps.t: If you want cameras, talk to them first
steps.d: If they can make the decision, they must agree. If they can't, any camera must be in their best interests and the least intrusive option. Involve family and anyone with a health and welfare Power of Attorney.

steps.t: Keep cameras out of private rooms
steps.d: Don't put cameras in bedrooms or bathrooms. Avoid recording sound unless there's a clear reason, as it's more intrusive.
Let care workers and the agency know where cameras are and why. Recording people without telling them damages trust.

steps.t: Keep the cameras private and secure
steps.d: Change the default password and turn on two-step login. If a camera films beyond their property, such as the street or a neighbour's garden, data protection law applies, so point cameras inside the home.

kits.name: Leaving hospital
kits.what: Make sure the right help is in place at home.

steps.t: Ask who is planning the discharge
steps.d: Ask the ward for the name of the person coordinating it, and for the discharge plan.

steps.t: Be clear about what you can do
steps.d: If you can't provide care, say so. Don't let the plan assume family will cover. Ask for a carer's assessment for yourself too.

steps.t: Ask to be their named contact
steps.d: Ask the ward to record you as their next of kin or main contact, so they keep you updated. Staff can only share details if they agree, or if it's in their best interests when they can't decide.
Ask about reablement or intermediate care to help them recover at home.
If health needs are complex, ask for the Continuing Healthcare checklist before discharge.
Make sure equipment such as a commode or raised toilet seat is delivered before they come home.
Ask for a list of medicines, who will collect them, and whether the pharmacy can provide blister packs.

Make sure the GP has the discharge letter, ask for your own copy, and ask whether a district nurse will visit. If they agree, the GP surgery can give you proxy access in the NHS App to see letters and order repeat prescriptions.

kits.name: Claiming Attendance Allowance
kits.what: Up to £114.60 a week if they're over State Pension age and need help. Savings and income don't matter.

steps.d: They must be over State Pension age and have needed help or supervision for at least 6 months because of an illness or disability. It's about the help they need, not whether anyone gives it.

Call the Attendance Allowance helpline on 0800 731 0122. If the form is returned within 6 weeks, payment is backdated to the day you called, so note the date. A downloaded form only counts from the day DWP receives it.
For a week, note each time they need help or someone keeping an eye on them, day and night, and how long it takes. Include falls, confusion and help at night.

steps.t: Answer for most days, including bad days
steps.d: Describe how things usually are, not their best day. Say what happens without help, such as a fall or a missed meal.
"Needs help getting out of the bath, about 20 minutes each morning" says more than "struggles with washing".
£76.70 a week for help in the day or at night. £114.60 a week for help both day and night, or if they're terminally ill.
Include copies, not originals, of letters from the GP, hospital or occupational therapist if you have them, and name a professional who knows them.
If they may not live more than 12 months, ask their doctor or nurse for form SR1. The claim is dealt with faster and paid at the higher rate.
They sign it, or you can if you're their appointee or attorney. Keep a copy of everything you send.
An award can mean extra Pension Credit, a Council Tax reduction and Carer's Allowance for you. Use the benefits calculator.
Ask for a mandatory reconsideration within one month of the decision letter. Citizens Advice Adviceline (England) 0800 144 8848 can help.

kits.name: Claiming Carer's Allowance
kits.what: £86.45 a week if you care 35 hours or more and earn £204 a week or less. Check first, as it can affect their benefits.

steps.d: You care for them at least 35 hours a week, and they get a qualifying benefit such as Attendance Allowance or the daily living part of PIP. You don't need to live with them or be related.
After tax, National Insurance and half of any pension contributions, you must earn £204 a week or less (2026). Going even slightly over stops the whole payment for that week.
If they get the severe disability extra in Pension Credit or other benefits, your Carer's Allowance can stop it. Ask Citizens Advice first: 0800 144 8848.
If your State Pension is more than £86.45 a week, Carer's Allowance won't be paid on top. Claiming can still add a carer amount to Pension Credit or Housing Benefit, so it's worth checking.
Use GOV.UK (search "apply for Carer's Allowance"). Have their National Insurance number, your bank details and recent payslips ready. It can be backdated up to 3 months.

steps.t: Can't get it? Claim Carer's Credit
steps.d: If you care for 20 hours a week or more, Carer's Credit protects your State Pension, even if you can't get Carer's Allowance.
Tell the Carer's Allowance Unit if your earnings or hours change, or if they go into hospital or a care home, to avoid being overpaid.
Carers UK 0808 808 7777. Citizens Advice Adviceline (England) 0800 144 8848.

kits.name: Making a Lasting Power of Attorney
kits.what: Lets someone they trust make decisions if they can't. Do it while they still can. England and Wales.

steps.d: Property and financial affairs covers the bank, bills and the house. Health and welfare covers care, treatment and where they live. Many families make both.
They must understand what it means when they sign. If you're not sure they still can, see the No Lasting Power of Attorney kit.
One or more people they trust, aged 18 or over. Decide whether attorneys must make every decision together (jointly) or can also act alone (jointly and severally).
A replacement attorney steps in if an attorney can no longer act.
Use GOV.UK (search "make a lasting power of attorney"). You can fill it in with them, but the choices must be theirs. Paper forms are available too.
Someone who has known them for at least 2 years, or a professional such as their GP or a solicitor, confirms they understand it and aren't under pressure. It can't be a family member or an attorney.
They sign first, then the certificate provider, then the attorneys. Signatures need a witness, and an attorney can't witness their signature.
£92 for each LPA, so £184 for both (2026). There's a reduction if their income is under £12,000, and an exemption on some benefits.
Registration takes 8 to 10 weeks if there are no mistakes. A mistake can mean starting again, so check every page before sending.
Use the online service (search "use a lasting power of attorney") to share it with banks, the GP and care providers. Keep the paper copy safe.
Office of the Public Guardian 0300 456 0300. Age UK 0800 678 1602.

kits.name: NHS Continuing Healthcare
kits.what: If their needs are mainly health needs, the NHS pays for all their care, at home or in a care home. England.

steps.d: Care fully funded by the NHS for people whose main need is a health need. It isn't means-tested. It depends on how complex, intense or unpredictable their needs are, not on a diagnosis.
Ask a nurse, social worker or the GP to complete the NHS Continuing Healthcare checklist. In hospital, ask before they're discharged. It's a short screening step.

If the checklist is positive, a team of professionals assesses them using the Decision Support Tool, which looks at 12 areas such as breathing, eating, mobility, behaviour and medicines. The NHS aims to decide within 28 days.
You can be there. Bring a diary of their needs over a few weeks, day and night, and any care records. Say if you think something has been missed.
If they're near the end of life and getting worse quickly, a doctor or nurse can use the fast-track route so care can start within days.
Ask for copies of the checklist, the Decision Support Tool and the decision letter.
Write to the Integrated Care Board (ICB) within 6 months of the decision to ask for a review. If you're still unhappy, ask NHS England for an independent review.
In a nursing home, they may get NHS-funded Nursing Care, a weekly NHS payment towards nursing costs. Ask about it.
If they get it, it's reviewed after 3 months and then at least once a year.
Age UK 0800 678 1602. Citizens Advice Adviceline (England) 0800 144 8848.

kits.name: Applying for a Blue Badge
kits.what: Parking closer to where they need to go. England's rules.

steps.d: They do if they get the higher rate mobility part of DLA; PIP with 8 points or more for "moving around"; PIP with 10 points for descriptor E under "planning and following journeys"; are registered blind (severely sight impaired); or get War Pensioners' Mobility Supplement or certain Armed Forces compensation. Attendance Allowance on its own doesn't count.

steps.t: If not, they may still qualify
steps.d: The council decides. For example, if walking is very difficult because of pain, breathlessness or the time it takes, or isn't safe for them. Non-visible conditions can count too, such as being a serious risk near traffic, struggling severely to plan or follow a journey, or becoming extremely anxious in public places.

A recent head-and-shoulders digital photo. A photo or scan of proof of identity (birth certificate, passport or driving licence) and proof of address (Council Tax bill or a recent government letter). Their National Insurance number, any benefit award letter (for PIP, the scores), and the current badge details if renewing.

steps.t: Get medical evidence, if they don't qualify automatically
steps.d: Check the council's own Blue Badge page first, as each council asks for different evidence. Many want letters from a consultant, specialist nurse, physiotherapist or occupational therapist, dated in the last 12 months. The letters should say how the condition affects walking or journeys, not just the diagnosis, how long it's likely to last, and what treatment has been tried. Letters about the outcome of an appointment count; appointment letters don't. Some councils say a GP letter alone isn't enough, and some professionals charge for letters.

steps.t: Getting their medical letters as their carer
steps.d: Hospital and clinic letters are usually copied to the GP. They can ask the GP surgery for copies of letters in their record, which is normally free. If they agree, the surgery can also give you proxy access in the NHS App so you can see their letters and record yourself; most surgeries ask you both to sign a consent form and show photo ID. If they can't make the decision themselves, a health and welfare Lasting Power of Attorney helps, and the GP decides what's appropriate.

steps.t: Write down how getting about affects them
steps.d: The form asks about their conditions and treatment, how far they can walk and how long it takes, what help they need, and the healthcare professionals involved in their care. Have their medicines list and the names of their GP, consultants and therapists to hand. A note of a typical trip, such as to the shops or the GP, makes this easier.
Use GOV.UK: gov.uk/apply-blue-badge. You can apply on their behalf, and save and come back later. Or ask the council for a paper form.
Up to £10 in England. The council tells you how to pay.
Usually within 12 weeks. The council may ask for more information, or invite them to a mobility assessment with an independent health professional. Keep copies of everything you send.
Ask the council to reconsider, explaining anything they missed. You can reapply if things change. Citizens Advice can help: Adviceline (England) 0800 144 8848.
The badge is theirs: use it only when they're travelling in the car, as driver or passenger. Show it on the dashboard, with the clock where needed. Misuse can mean a fine of up to £1,000.
Badges usually last up to 3 years, and you must reapply before it runs out. In Calendar, choose Reminder, then Blue Badge renewal, and it will remind you 12 weeks before.

kits.name: No Lasting Power of Attorney?
kits.what: When they can no longer decide: deputyship, appointees and best-interests decisions. England and Wales.

steps.t: Check for an older power of attorney
steps.d: An Enduring Power of Attorney made before October 2007 can still be used, but it must be registered with the Office of the Public Guardian once they can't manage. You can ask the Office of the Public Guardian to search its registers, free, to check for an LPA, EPA or deputy.

steps.t: Check whether they could still make an LPA
steps.d: Capacity depends on the decision and can vary from day to day. If they might still understand, ask the GP or a solicitor whether they could make one now. It's quicker and cheaper than the court route.

steps.t: Only benefits and pension? Become their appointee
steps.d: If their income is just State Pension and benefits, call the helpline for the benefit and ask to become their appointee. It's free. The DWP visits them and interviews you first. It doesn't cover bank savings or property.

steps.t: Savings, pensions or property? Apply to be their deputy
steps.d: A property and financial affairs deputy is appointed by the Court of Protection, usually a family member. Apply on GOV.UK (search "become a deputy"), online or by post. You'll need it to run their bank accounts, pay care fees from savings and usually to sell their home.
Form COP3 is completed by their GP or another professional, confirming they can't make these decisions. The court may not accept the application without it. The GP may charge for this.

steps.t: Tell them, and 3 people who know them
steps.d: You must visit them and explain the application, and give them forms COP14PADep and COP5. Send form COP15PADep and COP5 to at least 3 people who know them, such as relatives or their social worker. They have 14 days to reply, and you must apply within 3 months of telling them.
The application fee is £432 (2026). Help with the fee depends on their finances: ask about form COP44A.

It often takes several months. If something is urgent, such as care fees that must be paid, ask the court about an urgent interim order. Tell the care home or council that the application is in progress.

You may need to buy a security bond first. There's a one-off £100 assessment fee and a yearly supervision fee (£320, or £35 if they have under £21,000), and you send a report to the Office of the Public Guardian each year. Keep their money separate from yours and keep receipts.

These usually don't need a court application. Doctors, nurses and social workers decide in their best interests under the Mental Capacity Act and must consult family. Tell them you want to be involved. Health and welfare deputies are rarely appointed.

steps.t: If they move into a care home
steps.d: If they're under continuous supervision and not free to leave, the home must apply to the council for a Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards (DoLS) authorisation. You should be consulted, and you can ask questions or ask for a review. If there's no family, an independent advocate is appointed.

Office of the Public Guardian 0300 456 0300. Court of Protection 0300 456 4600. Alzheimer's Society 0333 150 3456. Citizens Advice Adviceline (England) 0800 144 8848. A solicitor who does Court of Protection work can apply for you, for a fee.

kits.name: Before you sign a care home contract

steps.d: Ask for it before moving day, and take time to read it. Check who is signing and in what role: only sign as their attorney if you have a Lasting Power of Attorney, and don't agree to pay fees personally unless you mean to.
What is the weekly fee, and what costs extra, such as hairdressing, trips or toiletries?
How often do fees rise, by how much, and how much notice do they give?
If the council starts paying later, will someone need to pay a top-up? Who agrees to it?

steps.t: Check deposits and payment in advance
steps.d: How much, and when is it returned?
How much notice is needed to leave, and how many days of fees are charged after a death?

steps.t: Check when a resident can be asked to leave
steps.d: Ask what the reasons are and what notice they give.
Ask for the complaints process. If it isn't resolved, you can go to the Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman.

steps.t: Get free help if anything is unclear
steps.d: Citizens Advice can explain your rights on fees, notice and unfair terms. Call the Citizens Advice consumer helpline on 0808 223 1133, or the Adviceline (England) on 0800 144 8848.

reminders.label: Blue Badge renewal
reminders.title: Renew the Blue Badge
reminders.details: The Blue Badge expires soon. Reapply before it runs out at gov.uk/apply-blue-badge. Have a recent photo, proof of identity and address, and any benefit award letter ready.

reminders.label: Attendance Allowance or PIP review
reminders.due: Award end or review date (on the award letter)
reminders.title: Attendance Allowance or PIP review coming up
reminders.details: Look out for the review form from the Department for Work and Pensions and send it back by the date given. Citizens Advice (0800 144 8848) can help with the form.

reminders.label: Chase a benefit claim
reminders.due: Date to chase if there's no decision
reminders.title: Chase the benefit claim
reminders.details: If there's no decision yet, call the benefit's helpline with the claim reference and National Insurance number. Note who you spoke to and what they said.

reminders.label: Council financial reassessment
reminders.title: Council care charges reassessment
reminders.details: The council reviews care charges each year. Gather bank statements, pension and benefit letters. Ask for the result in writing.

reminders.label: Care plan or needs review
reminders.title: Care plan review due
reminders.details: The council should review the care and support plan at least once a year, or sooner if needs change. Note what's working and what isn't, and ask for the review if it hasn't been booked.

reminders.label: Carer's assessment review
reminders.due: Date of your last carer's assessment
reminders.title: Ask for a carer's assessment review
reminders.details: Ask the council to review your carer's assessment, especially if caring has become harder or your work has changed. It's free.

reminders.label: Care fee increase
reminders.title: Care fees are going up
reminders.details: Check the new weekly fee against the contract, and whether savings still cover it. If the council pays part, ask whether a top-up will change. Citizens Advice consumer helpline: 0808 223 1133.

reminders.label: Council tax discount check
reminders.due: Date the new council tax bill arrives (usually March)
reminders.title: Check the council tax discount
reminders.details: Check the new bill still shows any discount, disregard or exemption, such as for severe mental impairment or for a carer. Call the council if it's missing.

reminders.label: Lasting Power of Attorney follow-up
reminders.due: Date to check on the registration
reminders.title: Check the Lasting Power of Attorney registration
reminders.details: If you haven't heard from the Office of the Public Guardian, contact them with the reference number to check progress.

reminders.label: Test the fall alarm and smoke alarms
reminders.title: Test the alarms
reminders.details: Press the fall alarm pendant's test button, or call the alarm company to test it. Press the test button on smoke and carbon monoxide alarms. Replace batteries if needed.

When is the next medicines review?

Can we be referred to the local falls service?
stroke: What rehabilitation is available at home?
Can we be referred to the Stroke Association's support service?
eol: Can we be referred to the palliative care team or local hospice?
Who do we call out of hours?
heart: Can we be referred to a heart failure nurse?
Who do we call if things change?
copd: Can we be referred to pulmonary rehabilitation?
Is there a respiratory nurse we can contact?
cancer: Who is our clinical nurse specialist?
What support is there for family, such as Macmillan?
sight: Can we be referred to the council's sensory support team?
When is the next sight or hearing test due?
continence: Can we be referred to the NHS continence service?
Are pads or other products available on the NHS?
diabetes: When are the next checks due?
arthritis: Which type of arthritis is it, and do we need a specialist?
Can we be referred to physiotherapy or an occupational therapist?
afterfall: Can we be referred to the falls service?
delirium: What happens next, and what should we watch for?
Who do we contact if it happens again?

questions.name: Visiting a care home
items: Do you have a vacancy, and when?
What is the weekly fee, and what costs extra?
How often do fees go up, and by how much?
Will you accept the council's rate if savings run out? Would a top-up be needed?
How many staff are on duty in the day and at night?

questions.name: Choosing a home care agency
items: What is your hourly rate? Is it higher at evenings and weekends?
What is the shortest visit you do?
Will the same carers come each time?
What happens if a carer is late or can't come?
What training do your carers have, for example in dementia care or moving and handling?

questions.name: Council needs assessment
items: When will the assessment happen, and who will do it?
Can I be there?
Can I have a carer's assessment too?
What support could be offered?
Could they have reablement first?

questions.name: Leaving hospital
items: When is the planned discharge date?
What support will be in place at home, and from when?
Is reablement or intermediate care available?
Will any equipment be delivered before they come home?
Should they be assessed for NHS continuing healthcare?

questions.name: GP or hospital appointment
items: What happens next?
Who is our main contact, and how do we reach them?
When is the next review?
What should we do if things change?
Can we have a copy of any letters?

questions.q: Is the person you care for over State Pension age?
Have they needed help with personal care or supervision for 6 months or more?
Is their income mainly the State Pension?
How many hours a week do you spend caring?
Do you earn more than £204 a week after tax and expenses?
